The Council of Life

CIRCLE 240 · 9–15 NOVEMBER 2026

1 · The Ginkgo at Rokeby

ANCIENT FRIEND of yOur Blooming Week

An ancient lineage in gold

A lineage that outlived the dinosaurs, still turning gold each autumn.

THE LIVING COMPANION

One ginkgo (Ginkgo biloba) standing alone on open lawn, its broad trunk dividing low into great spreading limbs. This tree's own age is not known. Its lineage is ancient: fossil ginkgo leaves more than 200 million years old have been found. Native to China, ginkgo is endangered in the wild.

LIVING SCIENCE & CARE

One individual tree, mapped in the Ancient Friends atlas; its age has not been measured or recorded. Fallen seeds have a fleshy coat that smells of rancid butter as it decays; do not eat or forage them.

THIS WEEK’S REFLECTION

2 · Hornbeam

TREE COMPANION of yOur Blooming Week

Strength in the grain

A quiet keeper of strength and shelter, through every turning season.

THE LIVING COMPANION

European hornbeam (Carpinus betulus) is a deciduous tree with pale grey bark and, with age, a fluted, twisted trunk. Its oval leaves have finely double-toothed edges. Its pale timber is extremely hard, and was once used for butchers' blocks, mill cogs and piano hammers.

LIVING SCIENCE & CARE

Beech or hornbeam? Hornbeam leaves are double-toothed; beech leaves have wavy edges. A clipped hornbeam hedge keeps its dry leaves through winter, giving birds shelter. Not an identification guide.

3 · Rosemary

PLANT COMPANION of yOur Blooming Week

A fragrance for remembering

An evergreen herb of scent, bees and long remembrance.

THE LIVING COMPANION

Rosemary (Salvia rosmarinus, formerly Rosmarinus officinalis) is an aromatic evergreen shrub. Its narrow, dark green leaves are pale and felty beneath. Small blue flowers open from mid-spring to summer, sometimes again in autumn, and feed pollinators.

LIVING SCIENCE & CARE

A culinary herb. The RHS notes it is a skin allergen, so wear gloves when pruning if your skin is sensitive. Grow it in full sun and well-drained soil; take semi-ripe cuttings in summer.

4 · Tomato Seed

Seed Companion of yOur Blooming Week

A summer kept for spring

A whole summer folded small, waiting for spring.

THE LIVING COMPANION

Tomato (Solanum lycopersicum) seeds are small, flattened and covered in fine hairs. Inside each, a curled embryo lies within its food store under a protective coat. A ripe fruit holds many seeds, each wrapped in jelly-like gel.

LIVING SCIENCE & CARE

Save seed from ripe fruit of an open-pollinated variety; F1 hybrids do not come true. Ferment seeds in their gel for a few days, rinse, dry fully and store cool and dry. Sow indoors at about 18°C.

THIS WEEK’S REFLECTION

Illustration · Sources: RHS · Brooklyn Botanic Garden · 3D Seed Cellar model is an illustrative, enlarged seed

5 · Field Maple

Leaf Companion of yOur Blooming Week

Gold in the hedgerow

Britain's own maple, turning the hedges to gold.

THE LIVING COMPANION

Field maple (Acer campestre) is the UK's only native maple. Its small, dark green leaves have five lobes with rounded teeth, and fade to rich gold in autumn. Its paired winged seeds, tinged pink, are set almost in a straight line.

LIVING SCIENCE & CARE

Field maple leaves are smaller and more rounded than sycamore or Norway maple, and older twigs often bear corky ridges. Its spring flowers feed bees. Not an identification guide.

6 · Calendula

Flower Companion of yOur Blooming Week

A little sun in the garden

Pot marigold: easy, edible and bright into autumn.

THE LIVING COMPANION

Pot marigold (Calendula officinalis) is an easy hardy annual with orange or yellow daisy-like flowers from summer into early autumn. Bees and hoverflies visit its open flowers. The petals are edible, with a slightly peppery taste.

LIVING SCIENCE & CARE

Save the curled brown seeds when dry; it often self-seeds. Traditionally used on skin, but clinical evidence is limited and mixed: not medical advice. Not French marigold (Tagetes).

7 · Medlar

Fruit Companion of yOur Blooming Week

Sweetness through patience

An old orchard fruit that sweetens only with waiting.

THE LIVING COMPANION

Medlar (Mespilus germanica) is a small, broad orchard tree of the rose family. Its russet fruits, crowned with long sepals, are picked hard in October or November and then 'bletted': stored until soft, brown and sweet.

LIVING SCIENCE & CARE

Blet on trays, stalks up, not touching, somewhere cool, dark and airy for two or three weeks. Bletted flesh is evenly soft and brown. Discard any fruit with mould, a sour or alcoholic smell, or split skin.

8 · Horn of Plenty

Fungus Companion of yOur Blooming Week

Hidden partners of the forest floor

A dark trumpet in the leaves, partnered with the trees.

THE LIVING COMPANION

Horn of plenty (Craterellus cornucopioides), or black trumpet, forms hollow, dark grey funnels with no gills. It grows in leaf litter in broadleaf woods, often under beech or oak, in partnership with tree roots, from late summer to autumn.

LIVING SCIENCE & CARE

Never eat a wild mushroom identified from a picture or this card: foraging needs expert, in-person identification. It dries well for cooking. Medicinal claims are unproven.

9 · Return of the Bird Tribes

Book Companion of yOur Blooming Week

Ken Carey · a vision of returning wings

A visionary book about belonging to the living Earth.

THE LIVING COMPANION

Return of the Bird Tribes is a visionary book by the American writer Ken Carey, first published in the late 1980s as part of his Starseed series. Its author presents it as received spiritual teaching about humanity's bond with the Earth.

LIVING SCIENCE & CARE

Spiritual and literary perspective, not history or ethnography, and not Indigenous teaching. Seek out Indigenous authors for their own traditions. No text is reproduced here.

10 · Sea Eagle

Bird Companion of yOur Blooming Week

Wide wings over wild water

The great 'flying barn door' returned to our skies.

THE LIVING COMPANION

The white-tailed eagle (Haliaeetus albicilla) is the UK's largest bird of prey, with a wingspan of 2 to 2.4 metres. Adults have a pale head, a huge yellow bill and a short, white, wedge-shaped tail. It eats mainly fish.

LIVING SCIENCE & CARE

Lost as a UK breeding bird by 1916, it returned through reintroduction: Rum from 1975, the Isle of Wight from 2019. Specially protected: watch from afar; never disturb a nest.
